- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >70), model often overshoots in next 3–5 days; apply downward correction of 2–5% for 3–7 day horizon.
- If official supply net is negative and bearish sentiment dominates (≥0.67), model underestimates downside risk; add 1–3% downward bias to forecast.
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.33–0.67), model exhibits mean reversion bias — forecast should be closer to recent 7-day average, not extrapolated trend.
- For 30-day forecasts, if recent 18-day history shows volatility >10% or sentiment swings, model overfits trend; use 10–15% smoothing or adjust for event-driven volatility.
- If official events are clustered (e.g., 3+ auctions in 7 days), model tends to ignore supply shock; reduce forecast by 1–3% per auction event in 7-day window.
- When bullish sentiment is high but true outcome is bearish (e.g., 70+ → 65–70), model fails to adjust; apply “sentiment-to-price” lag correction: if sentiment >0.67, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% per day until sentiment drops.
